Join YNRL

PhD, postdoc, and visiting opportunities for Fall 2024.

How to Apply (PhD)

YNRL admits PhD students through the Yale Department of Computer Science. There is no separate lab application — please apply to the Yale CS PhD program and indicate Prof. Aditi Ramaswamy as a faculty of interest in your statement of purpose.

Application deadline: December 15, 2023 (11:59pm ET) for Fall 2024 entry. Apply via the Yale Graduate School application portal.
What We Look For
  • Strong mathematical and machine-learning foundations (linear algebra, probability, optimization).
  • Systems depth (CUDA, distributed training, large-scale data pipelines) or linguistic depth (formal semantics, syntax, pragmatics).
  • Prior research output: a workshop paper, conference submission, open-source release, or strong undergraduate thesis.
  • A clear articulation of a research question you would want to spend five years on.
  • Comfort with collaborative, reading-group-driven scholarship.
Note: we read every statement of purpose carefully. Please do not use generic templates.

Frequently Asked Questions

Q. Is the GRE required?
A. No. Yale CS has made the GRE optional indefinitely. Scores submitted will not be held against an applicant, but they are not necessary.
Q. What is the funding situation?
A. Admitted PhD students receive a five-year guarantee of full tuition, stipend, and health insurance through a combination of fellowships, RA, and TA appointments.
Q. Should I email Prof. Ramaswamy before applying?
A. A brief, specific email referencing one of our recent papers is welcome but not required. Generic "I'm interested in your lab" emails will not receive a reply due to volume.
Q. What is the lab culture like?
A. Weekly reading group, biweekly 1:1s with the PI, paper-writing collaboration across subgroups, low hierarchy. We expect students to develop independent research agendas by year two.
Q. Are summer internships allowed?
A. Yes, starting after the second year. We encourage internships at industry labs (Google, Anthropic, Microsoft Research, Allen AI) when the project complements the student's thesis.
Q. Can I work remotely?
A. PhD students are expected to be resident in New Haven during the academic year. Short remote stints (conferences, family, collaborations) are normal. Postdocs and visiting researchers may negotiate hybrid arrangements.

Open Positions — Fall 2024

We have three confirmed openings for the 2024 cycle. Cross-listed projects (e.g., interpretability of multimodal models) are also welcome.

PhD · Fall 2024

Interpretability of Large Language Models

Advisor: A. Ramaswamy · 5-yr funded

Circuit-level analysis of refusal, factuality, and arithmetic in 7B-70B models. Builds on EMNLP 2023 Best Paper Runner-Up work.

PhD · Fall 2024

Multimodal Reasoning

Advisor: A. Ramaswamy · 5-yr funded

Pixel-faithful alignment, video-question answering with temporal scene graphs, and grounded compositional generalization.

Postdoc · 2-Year

Robust Evaluation of Foundation Models

NSF SAFRON · start: Summer/Fall 2024

Develop adversarial and distribution-shift benchmarks for frontier LMs. PhD in CS, statistics, or related field required.

Visiting Researchers

Stays of 3–12 months

YNRL hosts a small number of senior PhD students (third year and beyond) and faculty on sabbatical each year. Visitors are embedded in an active project, attend lab meetings, and typically co-author at least one paper during their stay.

We provide desk space at AKW Hall, library and compute access, and informal mentorship from the PI. Visitors must arrange their own funding (institutional sabbatical support, Fulbright, JSPS, etc.) and visa sponsorship through Yale OISS.

Inquiries: ynrl-visiting@cs.yale.edu — please attach a CV and a one-page research proposal. Read about current visitors →

Yale NLP & Reasoning Lab
Department of Computer Science
Research People Publications Code & Data News Join Us
Yale University
Research

Research Areas

Four interconnected threads on language, reasoning, and trustworthy AI — building language models that reason, explain, and remain robust.
Thread 01 · Foundations

Large Language Models

We study the architectural and algorithmic foundations of large autoregressive language models — with a particular focus on how sparse computation, attention routing, and chain-structured decoding affect a model's ability to perform faithful multi-step reasoning. Our work spans pre-training experiments at the 1B–13B scale and post-hoc analyses of frontier systems.

Key Papers
A. Ramaswamy, J. Liu, H. Park. Chain-of-Verification Decoding for Multi-Step Reasoning. NeurIPS 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2310.04521] [Code]
D. Alvarez, A. Ramaswamy. Sparse Attention Routing for 70B Models. ICML 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2305.18114] [Code]
H. Park, A. Ramaswamy. Scratchpad Faithfulness Under Tool Use. ICLR 2024
[PDF] [arXiv:2401.09833]
FIG. 1 — Training/inference loop with chain-of-verification decoding.
Thread 02 · Grounding

Multimodal Learning

We develop vision-language systems that are pixel-faithful: capable of grounding linguistic claims to specific image regions, video frames, or temporal scene segments. Our approach combines dual-encoder pretraining, region-level contrastive objectives, and temporal scene graph supervision.

Key Papers
S. Okafor, A. Ramaswamy. GroundCLIP: Pixel-Faithful Multimodal Alignment. ICCV 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2308.11192] [Code] [Data]
J. Liu, S. Okafor. VideoQA via Temporal Scene Graphs. CVPR 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2303.07765] [Code]
D. Alvarez, S. Okafor, A. Ramaswamy. OpenGroundVL: An Open Recipe for Grounded VLMs. ICLR 2024
[PDF] [arXiv:2402.03388]
FIG. 2 — Dual-encoder contrastive alignment with region-level supervision.
Thread 03 · Safety

Robustness

We study the failure modes of deployed language models under adversarial prompts, distribution shift, and prompt-injection. Our work develops both attacks — to surface real risk — and defenses, including instruction-tuned safety adapters and runtime monitors that detect jailbreak attempts before generation completes.

Key Papers
M. Feldman, A. Ramaswamy. PromptArmor: Runtime Defense Against Prompt Injection. USENIX Security 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2306.04188] [Code]
D. Alvarez, M. Feldman. Distribution Shift in Open-Ended Generation Benchmarks. EMNLP 2022
[PDF] [arXiv:2210.11904]
J. Liu, A. Ramaswamy. REASON-Bench: Stress-Testing Multi-Hop QA. NeurIPS 2023 D&B
[PDF] [arXiv:2310.16772] [Data]
FIG. 3 — Perturbation pipeline for stress-testing language models.
Thread 04 · Explanation

Interpretability

We reverse-engineer the computational mechanisms inside trained transformers — identifying attention heads, MLP neurons, and residual-stream circuits that implement specific behaviors. Recent work isolates the circuits responsible for refusal in instruction-tuned 7B models and traces how those circuits shift under fine-tuning.

Key Papers
A. Ramaswamy, W. Liu. Probing Refusal Circuits in 7B Language Models. EMNLP 2023 ★ Best Paper Runner-Up
[PDF] [arXiv:2311.02845] [Code]
W. Liu, H. Park. Attention Head Taxonomy via Causal Patching. ICLR 2023
[PDF] [arXiv:2302.07991]
A. Ramaswamy, M. Feldman. Yale Interpretability Toolkit: A Library for Mechanistic Analysis. JMLR-OSS 2023
[PDF] [Code]
FIG. 4 — Causal graph of refusal-relevant attention heads across 32 layers.

Ongoing Projects

Currently-active artifacts and benchmarks released by the lab.
Benchmark

REASON-Bench

A 12,400-question stress-test suite for multi-hop reasoning, covering arithmetic, planning, and counterfactual chains. Released under MIT license.

Model + Data

OpenGroundVL

An open recipe for region-grounded vision-language models trained on 18M image-region-caption triples. Checkpoints at 1.3B and 7B scales.

Evaluation

SAFRON-Eval

DARPA SAFRON-funded evaluation harness for adversarial robustness of frontier LMs, with automated red-team probes and reproducible scorecards.

Library

Yale Interpretability Toolkit

A Python library for causal patching, attribution, and circuit discovery on HuggingFace transformer models. v0.4 released October 2023.

content.text:
All 5 pages are written. Each is self-contained with embedded CSS (and inline SVG diagrams in place of bitmap images). Highlights:

- **home.html** — utility bar, brand+nav header, hero+quote, Research Focus, 3-card Publications, 2-card Open Positions, news log, CSS-illustrated lab group photo, 5 funder cards, 4-col footer.
- **people.html** — PI block with monogram tile, 6 PhD students in 3-col grid (colored monogram tiles), gold spotlight card, postdocs/research scientists/visitors, alumni table, SVG collaboration network diagram.
- **publications.html** — Year/Topic filter chips, papers grouped by year with venue badges and arXiv/PDF/code links.
- **research.html** — Four alternating-background threads (Foundations / Grounding / Safety / Explanation), each with an inline-SVG figure (training loop, dual-encoder, perturbation pipeline, attention-head graph) and Ongoing Projects grid.
- **join.html** — How-to-Apply card with yellow deadline callout, FAQ card, Open Positions 3-up, blue Visiting Researchers panel.

Shared visual language: Yale navy (#0a3161), red accent (#a02538), Source Serif 4 headings + Source Sans 3 body + JetBrains Mono for links/dates, ivory alternating section backgrounds.
